cards.open_question: Does passing NASA's 1-g flame propagation screening test show that a cabin material is acceptable in reduced gravity? SoFIE is designed to study this; FlameGuard-SI holds no SoFIE test-level results to answer it.
cards.title: Open question: does 1-g material screening cover reduced gravity?

member1_review.requested_change: Present as an open research question with the quotes, not as a FlameGuard-SI finding.
member1_review.applied: Retitled as an open question; presentation set to research_context; open_question added; interpretation reworded so it draws no conclusion.

cards.disclaimer: Qualitative research insight for discussion. Not a flight-qualified or certified fire-safety recommendation.

finding.statement: NASA sources say the 1-g flame propagation test in NASA-STD-6001 is considered by some researchers not to be conservative in low gravity, and list validating 1-g material selection for low-gravity fires as a SoFIE application. For SoFIE-GEL, NASA reports that observations agree with model-predicted trends.

interpretation.text: The quoted sources raise this as an open question; they do not settle it. FlameGuard-SI draws no conclusion until SoFIE test-level results are imported and reviewed.

implication.text: If the question is answered in the negative, material lists for lunar and Martian habitats would need reduced-gravity flammability evidence in addition to 1-g screening results.
implication.extrapolation_warning: SoFIE tests microgravity, not lunar or Martian gravity. Partial-gravity behaviour can differ from both 1 g and 0 g.

limitations: Built on stated objectives and a reported expert view, not on measured results.

cards.title: Low-flow flames can flare up when airflow increases

member1_review.verdict: accept as R3, once Member 3 curates m5-bass2-flow-flareup as a measured qualitative finding
member1_review.applied: Evidence quote trimmed to the observational clause; the authors' evaluation of danger and the unquoted 'dim and stable' detail removed from the finding and interpretation.

cards.disclaimer: Qualitative research insight for discussion. Not a flight-qualified or certified fire-safety recommendation.

finding.statement: BASS-II authors report that flames sustained at very low air flow speeds can flare up quickly with a sudden increase in air flow speed.

interpretation.text: In microgravity, forced airflow supplies oxygen to the flame. In BASS-II, a flame sustained at low flow could intensify quickly when the flow increased.

implication.text: Fire-response research for habitats and rovers could study how restarting or increasing ventilation affects a small fire. This needs study; it is not a procedure.
implication.extrapolation_warning: On the Moon, buoyant flow exists at reduced strength, so low-flow microgravity behaviour may not appear the same way.

limitations: Small samples in a small duct; not habitat-scale fires.
Flow speeds and test ids behind the statement are not imported.

cards.title: CO2 and CO rose more significantly than temperature and pressure in Saffire tests

member1_review.requested_change: Do not compare quantities with different units ('larger signal'); keep the source's own framing. Add that Saffire burned in a large uncrewed vehicle, not a habitat atmosphere.
member1_review.applied: Title and interpretation now use the source's wording; the cross-unit comparison was removed; a limitation about the uncrewed vehicle and atmosphere was added.

cards.disclaimer: Qualitative research insight for discussion. Not a flight-qualified or certified fire-safety recommendation.

finding.statement: Preliminary Saffire results report that the spacecraft temperature and pressure rise were less significant than the increase in CO2 and CO. In BASS-II, the CO-CO2 relationship was linear for some datasets but not for all fuel geometries and flows.

interpretation.text: As the Saffire authors put it, the temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide. In BASS-II the CO-CO2 relationship depended on fuel geometry and flow, so one fixed ratio may not describe every fire.

implication.text: Fire-detection research for habitats could include combustion-product monitoring (CO, CO2) and test how fuel type affects it. No detection time, warning time or false-alarm rate is claimed.
implication.extrapolation_warning: Both sources are microgravity tests. On the Moon or Mars, buoyant convection and habitat atmosphere change how combustion products spread to sensors.

limitations: Saffire VI results are described by the source as preliminary.
Saffire burned inside a large uncrewed Cygnus vehicle after it left the ISS, not in a crewed habitat atmosphere.
BASS-II gas readings were taken before and after each test, not continuously.
No sensor response times are imported.

cards.open_question: Are some habitat materials more flammable, or able to burn at lower oxygen concentrations, in lunar gravity than on Earth? This is the hypothesis FM2 is designed to test; no lunar measurement is in FlameGuard-SI.
cards.title: Hypothesis under test: lunar gravity may raise flammability for some materials

member1_review.requested_change: Keep it labelled as a hypothesis (FM2).
member1_review.applied: Title starts with 'Hypothesis under test'; presentation set to research_context; open_question added; white-paper authors named.

cards.disclaimer: Qualitative research insight for discussion. Not a flight-qualified or certified fire-safety recommendation.

finding.statement: NASA researchers hypothesise that some materials are more flammable in lunar gravity than on Earth, and NASA's FM2 page says modelling and reduced-gravity experiments suggest materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity. A white paper by Ya-Ting Liao, Luca Carmignani, Justin Niehaus and Michael Gollner states that partial-gravity fire behaviour cannot be expected to be interpolated between normal-gravity and microgravity data.

interpretation.text: This is a hypothesis that FM2 is designed to test, not an established lunar result. Until lunar measurements exist, lunar flammability margins remain uncertain.

implication.text: If the hypothesis holds, lunar habitat material choices would carry more flammability uncertainty than 1-g screening suggests, especially near oxygen limits.
implication.extrapolation_warning: No lunar-surface combustion data is in this register. FM2 flight status and results were not verified.

limitations: Based on modelling and short-duration reduced-gravity tests described by the sources, not on lunar data.
No material-specific oxygen limits are imported.

cards.disclaimer: Qualitative research insight for discussion. Not a flight-qualified or certified fire-safety recommendation.

finding.statement: A decadal-survey white paper by Ya-Ting Liao, Luca Carmignani, Justin Niehaus and Michael Gollner (hosted on a NASA website) states that fire behaviour on the Moon and Mars cannot be expected to be interpolated between normal-gravity and microgravity data. The 'Fire on the Moon' concept plans to refine pressure-gravity scaling relations and apply them to other gravity levels. Saffire data showed enclosure size affected flame spread more than anticipated.

interpretation.text: None of the investigations in this register tested Martian gravity. Martian statements depend on scaling relations that are still planned, and Saffire shows fire behaviour can depend on factors such as enclosure size that are hard to scale.

implication.text: Any Mars habitat fire-safety claim in FlameGuard-SI should be labelled as extrapolated and list the gravity, atmosphere and enclosure assumptions it relies on.
implication.extrapolation_warning: No Martian-gravity or Martian-habitat combustion data is in this register.

limitations: A white-paper statement, a planned method and one reported result; no scaling relation is available.
Habitat atmosphere composition and pressure are not addressed by these sources.

cards.disclaimer: Qualitative research insight for discussion. Not a flight-qualified or certified fire-safety recommendation.

finding.statement: FLEX was designed to assess inert-gas suppressant effectiveness in microgravity for liquid droplets, and a NASA report presents results from its first 284 tests. NASA's combustion overview says putting out fires in space must consider flame geometry, material characteristics and extinguishing method, because ground methods could be ineffective or make the flame worse.

interpretation.text: Suppression evidence is specific to fuel phase, geometry and conditions. As Member 1's review notes, FLEX tested extinction in chamber atmospheres pre-diluted with inert gas, not a suppressant discharged onto an established fire. FLEX covers liquid droplets and BASS covers solids; their test-level results have not been imported, so no extinction values or suppressant comparisons are shown.

implication.text: Results from pre-diluted atmospheres should not be read as the performance of a suppressant discharged onto a fire, and should not be transferred between liquid-droplet and solid-material fires without compatible evidence.
implication.extrapolation_warning: Droplet tests in microgravity; suppression under lunar gravity with buoyant flow is not covered.

limitations: Liquid droplets, not solid habitat materials.

FLEX tested extinction in inert-gas pre-diluted atmospheres, not discharged suppressants (Member 1's review, citing the PR #4 atmosphere-composition columns). Member 5 has not yet checked this against the FLEX report; to be verified when the PR #4 data is reviewed.
The FLEX report's authors state they do not interpret the results.
